title: “THE TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH”—SO WHY DID PAUL USE GOD’S MARRIAGE VERSE TO DESCRIBE SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE?
paragraphs: “THE TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH”—SO WHY DID PAUL USE GOD’S MARRIAGE VERSE TO DESCRIBE SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE?

One of the most disturbing statements in the New Testament reveals something many Christians have never understood about sex, the human body, spiritual union, and the breathtaking mercy of Jesus Christ.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
But because of what it means when we finally do.

The apostle Paul took one of the most beautiful declarations ever spoken about marriage—words first uttered in the Garden of Eden, before sin entered the world—and applied them to a man having sex with a prostitute.
Read that again.
Words God gave to describe the union of husband and wife.
Words Jesus Himself would later affirm when teaching about marriage.
Paul used those very words while warning believers about sexual immorality.
Why?
Was Paul suggesting that sleeping with a prostitute makes someone married to her?
Was he saying every sexual encounter creates an unbreakable spiritual marriage?
Or was he revealing something far more unsettling about what happens when human beings take something God designed for covenant love and separate it from the covenant itself?
Because the answer is not merely about prostitutes in ancient Corinth.
It is about the person who thought a one-night stand meant nothing.
The married person who crossed a line and convinced themselves it was only physical.
The Christian who loves Jesus but keeps returning to pornography.
The believer carrying memories of someone they wish they had never slept with.
The person who feels permanently contaminated by what happened to their body.
And perhaps most painfully, the person who wonders whether God still wants them after everything they have done.
If any of those descriptions touch something you have tried to bury, stay with me.
Because Paul does not end this passage by telling broken people that their bodies are worthless.
He ends by declaring that they were bought with a price.
And that changes everything.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:16:
The original Greek is even more revealing.
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν; Ἔσονται γάρ, φησίν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.
A close translation reads:
“Or do you not know that the one joining himself to a prostitute is one body? For, He says, the two shall become one flesh.”
Notice something.
Paul does not merely say that the two people experience pleasure.
He says they become ἓν σῶμα (hen sōma)—“one body.”
Then he supports his argument by quoting Genesis 2:24.
This is where the uncomfortable question begins.
Why would Paul reach all the way back to Eden to explain something happening in the brothels of Corinth?
To understand his warning, we must first understand what God originally said.
Before betrayal.
Before prostitution.
Before pornography.
Before broken marriages, hidden affairs, sexual exploitation, and the countless ways humanity would wound itself through misused intimacy.
There was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was a God who looked at human loneliness and declared that it was not good for the man to be alone.
Genesis 2 describes God forming the woman and bringing her to the man.
Adam's response is not merely biological recognition.
It is a declaration of shared humanity and intimate belonging.
“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” (Genesis 2:23, ESV)
Then Scripture declares:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24, ESV)
In the Hebrew, the final phrase reads:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
“And they shall become one flesh.”
The word בָּשָׂר (basar) means “flesh.”
The word אֶחָד (echad) means “one.”
Together, basar echad expresses the profound bodily and relational unity of husband and wife.
But we must be careful.
The Hebrew phrase does not, by itself, describe a mystical substance passing between two people. Nor does it teach that two individuals lose their separate identities.
Genesis describes a new marital union in which two distinct persons become united in a shared life.
Sexual intimacy belongs within that larger covenant reality.
It is not the whole of marriage, but it is profoundly connected to marriage.
Jesus affirmed this understanding.
When questioned about divorce, He quoted Genesis and declared:
“So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” (Matthew 19:6, ESV)
Jesus was speaking about marriage.
A sacred joining.
A covenant relationship not intended to be casually discarded.
And yet Paul takes that same Genesis language and brings it into a radically different setting.
Not a wedding.
Not a faithful husband and wife.
A prostitute.
Why?
Because the Corinthians were living in a culture where sexual activity could be treated as something detached from moral responsibility.
Corinth was a prosperous Roman city shaped by commerce, social hierarchy, religious diversity, and familiar Greco-Roman sexual double standards.
Sexual exploitation and prostitution were part of that wider ancient world.

We should not exaggerate the evidence by repeating the popular but historically questionable story that Paul's Corinth operated a temple staffed by a thousand sacred prostitutes. That claim is often drawn from descriptions associated with an earlier period and cannot simply be applied to first-century Corinth.
The biblical argument is serious enough without embellishment.
Some believers in Corinth apparently needed to be reminded that freedom in Christ did not make every bodily appetite morally permissible.
Paul addresses the slogan:
“All things are lawful for me.” (1 Corinthians 6:12, ESV)
Then he answers:
“But not all things are helpful.”
And again:
“I will not be dominated by anything.”
That second statement matters.
Because something can begin as a choice and eventually become a master.
A secret habit.
A repeated compromise.
An appetite that demands more while promising satisfaction it cannot finally deliver.
Paul continues by addressing the body itself.
“The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.” (1 Corinthians 6:13, ESV)
That is an astonishing declaration.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
Your body is not disposable.
Your body is not simply a machine that carries around your real self.
Christianity does not teach that God only cares about your soul while ignoring what you do physically.
The Gospel is not an escape from the body.
It includes the redemption of the body.
Paul grounds this in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
“And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power.” (1 Corinthians 6:14, ESV)
Do you see what he is doing?
Before he speaks about prostitution, Paul speaks about resurrection.
Before he warns against sexual sin, he reminds believers that their bodies have an eternal future in God's redemptive purpose.
The body matters because Christ rose bodily.
The body matters because believers belong to Him.
The body matters because what we do with it cannot be separated from the One who redeemed us.
Then comes the sentence that would have shaken the Corinthian church:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:15, ESV)
Imagine hearing that for the first time.
Your body.
With its history.
Its weaknesses.
Its wounds.
Its desires.
Its scars.
Its memories.
A member of Christ.
Paul then asks whether he should take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute.
His answer is emphatic:
“Never!”
The Greek expression is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It communicates a forceful rejection: “May it never be!” or “Absolutely not!”
Paul is horrified by the contradiction.
Not because he thinks prostitutes are beyond God's mercy.
Not because he considers sexually exploited people less human.
Not because the human body is inherently filthy.
But because a person who belongs to Christ must not treat sexual union as morally meaningless.
The issue is not that sex is too dirty for God.
The issue is that sex is too significant to be treated as nothing.
And this brings us back to the question.
Why did Paul quote Genesis 2:24?
Because even when sexual intercourse occurs outside marriage, its bodily significance does not simply disappear.
Paul's argument depends on recognizing that sexual union is real, even when it occurs in a setting contrary to God's design.
But here we must distinguish what Scripture actually says from what Christians sometimes add to it.
Paul is not teaching that intercourse with a prostitute automatically creates a marriage covenant.
He does not call the prostitute the man's wife.
He does not instruct the man to regard the encounter as a legitimate marriage.
He does not teach that every sexual partner becomes a permanent spouse in God's sight.
Marriage in Scripture involves more than the physical act of intercourse. It is a covenantal union involving faithful commitment and the responsibilities of marriage.
What Paul does teach is that the physical act cannot be dismissed as spiritually or morally insignificant.
Sexual union is not identical to marriage.
But neither is it detached from the one-flesh reality for which God designed sexual intimacy.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because some people have been taught that every sexual encounter creates an indestructible supernatural bond that can only be broken through a special deliverance ceremony.
Others have been told that sexual sin permanently attaches pieces of their souls to previous partners.
Some live terrified that they can never truly belong to a future spouse because too much of themselves has already been given away.
But 1 Corinthians 6:16 does not explicitly teach those claims.
The Greek word translated “joined” is κολλώμενος (kollōmenos), from kollaō, meaning to join, cling, or attach.
It is a strong word.
It emphasizes genuine connection.
But the word itself does not prove the existence of an invisible, permanently binding spiritual chain.
Nor does Paul say that a believer who has sinned sexually must undergo a special ritual to retrieve fragments of their soul.
We should never make Scripture say less than it says.
But we must also refuse to make it say more.
Sexual sin can have profound consequences.
It can wound trust.
It can produce shame.
It can damage marriages.
It can expose people to disease, exploitation, or unwanted pregnancy.
It can shape patterns of attachment and desire.
It can leave memories that take time, wisdom, support, and healing to process.
Those consequences are real.
But they are not evidence that Jesus Christ is powerless to redeem a person's past.
And for someone reading this with tears in their eyes, that difference may be the difference between despair and hope.
Because perhaps you were taught that you were permanently ruined.
Perhaps someone told you that no faithful Christian would ever want you because of your sexual history.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that the worst thing you did is now the truest thing about you.
Or perhaps something was done to you without your consent, and you have been carrying shame that never belonged to you.
Hear this clearly.
Sexual assault is not the victim's sexual sin.
The Bible's call to repentance must never be turned into an accusation against someone who was violated.
The guilt belongs to the perpetrator, not the person who was harmed.
God does not demand that victims repent for violence committed against them.
And no person's worth is erased by what another person did to their body.
If you were violated, you are not spiritually contaminated by someone else's crime.
You deserve protection, compassion, justice, and care.
And if you willingly participated in sexual sin, the Gospel still does not tell you that your story is over.
It calls you to repentance.
And it offers you a Savior.
That is precisely where Paul's argument becomes breathtaking.
After warning against sexual immorality, he writes:
The Greek reads:
ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν.
Ho de kollōmenos tō kyriō hen pneuma estin.
“But the one joined to the Lord is one spirit.”
Notice the parallel.
The person joined to a prostitute becomes one body.
The person joined to the Lord becomes one spirit.
Paul is contrasting sexual union with the believer's relationship to Christ.
He is not claiming that union with Christ eliminates our personal identity or that believers become divine beings.
He is describing the profound spiritual belonging established through relationship with the Lord.
The believer belongs to Jesus.
And that belonging changes how the believer should live.
Here is the part we cannot afford to miss.
Paul's ultimate answer to sexual immorality is not simply, “Try harder to control yourself.”
It is, “Remember whose you are.”
Remember the Christ who died for you.
Remember the Lord who rose from the grave.
Remember the One who has called you into a new life.
Remember that your body is not an object without purpose.
You belong to Jesus.
And because you belong to Him, you are called to live differently.
This is why Paul commands:
“Flee from sexual immorality.” (1 Corinthians 6:18, ESV)
The Greek verb is φεύγετε (pheugete).
“Flee.”
Run away.
Do not negotiate with it.
Do not build a comfortable home beside temptation and expect yourself never to enter.
Do not keep feeding what you are praying God will help you overcome.
There are moments when spiritual maturity looks less like standing your ground and more like walking out the door.
Closing the browser.
Ending the conversation.
Deleting the secret account.
Refusing the invitation.
Confessing what has been hidden.
Seeking help instead of pretending you have everything under control.
And sometimes it means admitting that you have confused being desired with being loved.
That attention is not necessarily affection.
That physical access is not the same as covenant commitment.
That someone wanting your body does not automatically mean they are willing to honor your heart.
Some of the deepest wounds in people's lives began with the words, “It doesn't mean anything.”
But afterward, it meant something.
Not always in the same way.
Not always with the same emotional consequences.
Yet enough to leave a person asking why something they were told was casual became so difficult to forget.
Paul's teaching challenges the idea that human beings can completely separate physical intimacy from moral responsibility.
But it also challenges another destructive lie.
The lie that once you have sinned, you are no longer worth loving.
Because Paul's warning is not the final word.
Listen to what he says next.
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19, ESV)
A temple.
Think about that.
Not a garbage dump.
Not a disposable object.
Not a ruined building that God has abandoned.
A temple of the Holy Spirit.
Paul is speaking to believers about the indwelling presence of God.
He is not promising that Christians will never struggle again.
He is not denying that sin has consequences.
He is declaring that their bodies now belong to a holy purpose.
Then he gives the reason:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV)
Bought with a price.
What price?
The New Testament points us to the sacrificial death of Jesus Christ.
Peter writes that believers were ransomed not with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Paul himself teaches that Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Not a donation.
Not an offering.
Not a lifetime of religious performance.
It was the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Because Jesus did not die only for people with respectable histories.
He died for sinners.
People who lied.
People who betrayed.
People who used others.
People who broke promises.
People who worshiped their appetites.
People who lived double lives.
People who needed mercy more than they wanted to admit.
Earlier in the same letter, Paul describes the former lives of some Corinthian believers.
Among the sins he names are sexual immorality, adultery, theft, greed, drunkenness, and other forms of unrighteousness.
Then comes one of the most hope-filled sentences in the entire New Testament:
“And such were some of you.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, ESV)
Were.
One small word.
One enormous testimony.
Paul does not pretend their former sins never happened.
He does not deny the damage sin can cause.
He does not tell them that repentance is unnecessary.
He says something far greater.
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, ESV)
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
These are not sentimental words.
They describe the saving work of God in people who desperately needed grace.
The Greek word translated “washed” is ἀπελούσασθε (apelousasthe), from apolouō, meaning to wash away or wash clean.
The verse speaks of the decisive change associated with belonging to Christ.
The word “sanctified” points to being set apart for God.
The word “justified” speaks of being declared righteous before God.
And all of this is grounded in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and the work of God's Spirit.
Do you understand the beauty of that?
Paul did not write these words to people who had never sinned sexually.
He wrote them to a church that included people whose former lives had been marked by serious sin.
Their past was real.
But their past was not their final identity.
Jesus had rewritten their story.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending their actions were harmless.
But by saving sinners and bringing them into a new relationship with God.
This is what grace does.
Grace does not excuse sin.
Grace rescues sinners.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live for Christ (Titus 2:11–12).
Grace does not promise that every consequence will disappear overnight.
Grace promises that sin does not have to be the master of those who belong to Jesus (Romans 6:14).
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You may still remember what happened.
You may still grieve the choices you made.
You may still need to rebuild trust.
You may still need counseling, accountability, medical care, or time to heal.
Forgiveness does not erase the responsibility to make things right where possible.
But if you are in Christ, you do not have to spend the rest of your life treating your past as more powerful than His cross.
The cross is not fragile.
The resurrection is not weak.
And the mercy of Jesus is not reserved for people who have only made small mistakes.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8, a passage whose textual history requires care because the account is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel.
The story has been deeply influential in Christian tradition, but we should acknowledge that manuscript question rather than conceal it.
In the familiar account, a woman accused of adultery is placed before Jesus.
Her accusers want judgment.
Jesus exposes their hypocrisy.
And the story ends with His call to leave sin behind.
It is a picture of mercy joined with moral seriousness.
But we do not have to depend on a textually disputed passage to know that Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Luke 7 records Jesus receiving a woman known in the city as a sinner, while a Pharisee silently questions whether Jesus understands what kind of person is touching Him.
Jesus responds with a lesson about forgiveness and love.
He tells the woman:
“Your sins are forgiven.” (Luke 7:48, ESV)
And then:
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” (Luke 7:50, ESV)
What a difference between the way the world often labels people and the way Jesus receives those who come to Him in faith.
The world may remember the scandal.
Jesus brings the possibility of redemption.
The world may keep repeating what someone used to be.
The Gospel declares what God's grace can make them.
And that brings us to the heart of the entire passage.
Paul did not quote “the two shall become one flesh” to create hopelessness.
He quoted it to awaken believers to the sacred significance of their bodies and the seriousness of sexual union.
He wanted the Corinthians to understand that sexual behavior matters precisely because they matter.
Their bodies matter.
Their union with Christ matters.
Their obedience matters.
Their future resurrection matters.
And the price paid for their redemption matters.
If you are married, this passage calls you to honor your covenant, guard your fidelity, and treat your spouse as a person to love rather than an appetite to satisfy.
If you are single, it reminds you that your worth is not determined by whether someone desires you sexually.
If you are struggling with pornography, it calls you out of secrecy and toward repentance, accountability, and the freedom of living in the light.
If you have committed adultery, it calls you to stop justifying betrayal, turn from sin, and take responsibility for the harm you have caused.
If you have been sexually exploited or assaulted, it reminds you that another person's wrongdoing does not erase your dignity before God.
If you carry regret over past relationships, it invites you to bring that history honestly before Christ rather than build your entire identity around it.
And if you have fallen again after promising God you never would, do not confuse repentance with pretending your struggle is small.
Bring it into the light.
Confess your sin.
Seek help.
Take concrete steps to turn away.
And remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (ESV)
Not because confession earns salvation.
Not because tears purchase mercy.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior who has made forgiveness possible.
There is something deeply moving about the fact that Paul uses the language of joining twice.
Joined to a prostitute.
Joined to the Lord.
One speaks of a bodily union outside God's intended covenant.
The other speaks of the believer's spiritual union with Christ.
And the contrast forces a question that reaches far beyond ancient Corinth.
What are you allowing to shape your life when you already belong to Jesus?
What are you returning to when your heart knows it is destroying your peace?
What secret compromise have you been calling harmless because you are afraid to confront it?
What part of your life have you kept away from the Lord who gave His life for you?
These questions are not meant to entertain religious spectators.
They are meant to bring us before God.
Because it is possible to know the right verses and still live with a divided heart.
It is possible to post Scripture publicly while protecting sin privately.
It is possible to condemn the failures of others while hiding our own.
And it is possible to become so accustomed to grace as a theological word that we forget what it cost.
Jesus was crucified.
Not as a symbol of vague religious inspiration.
But as the Savior who bore our sins and rose victorious.
He did not purchase His people so that they could continue treating sin as their rightful master.
He redeemed them so they could belong to Him.
And belonging to Him is not imprisonment.
It is life.
Maybe this is the moment to stop pretending.
Maybe you need to tell your spouse the truth.
Maybe you need to ask a mature believer to pray with you.
Maybe you need to seek pastoral counsel.
Maybe you need to end a relationship that keeps pulling you away from obedience.
Maybe you need to stop punishing yourself for sins you have already confessed and genuinely turned away from.
Maybe you need to understand, for the first time, that holiness is not the price you pay to make Jesus love you.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by His grace.
And maybe you have never truly surrendered to Christ at all.
You have admired Him.
Quoted Him.
Listened to sermons about Him.
But never turned from sin and trusted Him as Savior and Lord.
The invitation of the Gospel is not to manufacture a respectable past.
It is to come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
He calls people to follow Him.
And He is able to save those who draw near to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
If this article has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to perform your confession for strangers on the internet.
But you do need to be honest before God.
If you have experienced the restoring mercy of Christ, consider sharing a testimony of what His grace has changed in your life.
Someone else may need to know that repentance and restoration are possible.
And if you are still fighting to walk faithfully with Jesus, do not mistake the presence of a battle for proof that you must surrender.
Keep bringing your life into the light.
Keep returning to Scripture.
Keep seeking the support of faithful believers.
Keep your eyes on Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn people's pain into religious entertainment.
Not to build an audience around shame.
But to help people encounter biblical truth, understand the Gospel, confront sin honestly, and grow in a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
There are people who will never enter a church building but may read a Scripture-centered article shared on Facebook.
There are struggling believers who may be one thoughtful message away from asking for help.
There are husbands and wives quietly praying for restoration.
There are young people surrounded by confusing messages about sexuality, identity, and love.
There are people who have been told that their past makes them unreachable.
And they need to hear the truth.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
His Word still exposes darkness.
His grace still calls people into the light.
A single share can place biblical encouragement before someone who would never have searched for it themselves.
And if you believe this kind of ministry is worth sustaining, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Some believers may choose to give from the portion of their finances they have set aside for Christian ministry. Others may see this as an additional monthly offering of support.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
“God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, ESV)
You do not have to pay to receive His grace.
And no financial contribution can purchase His favor.
The products are simply an expression of appreciation.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
To help believers open their Bibles again.
To help struggling Christians rediscover hope in Christ.
To help families talk about Scripture.
To encourage repentance without despair and holiness without self-righteousness.
To keep pointing people back to the crucified and risen Savior.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Speak the truth with love.
Point someone toward Jesus.
The goal is to see more people encounter the Gospel and grow in obedience to Christ.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the question that began this entire conversation.
Why did Paul apply the words “the two shall become one flesh” to sex with a prostitute?
Because what God designed for covenant intimacy cannot be reduced to a meaningless physical transaction.
Because our bodies matter.
Because sexual union carries moral significance even when people try to separate it from God's design.
Because those who belong to Christ are called to honor Him with their bodies.
And because the Gospel is not merely about what Jesus saves us from.
It is also about whom He saves us for.
Himself.
That is why the final command in 1 Corinthians 6 is so beautiful.
“So glorify God in your body.”
Not merely in your songs.
Not merely in your social media posts.
Not merely in your religious conversations.
In your body.
In your private decisions.
In your relationships.
In your integrity.
In the moments when nobody is watching.
In the choices that reveal whether Christ is only someone you admire or truly the Lord you follow.
And when you fail, do not run farther into darkness.
Turn back to Him.
The One who calls you to holiness is the same Savior who gave His blood for your redemption.
The One who exposes sin is the same Lord who offers forgiveness to repentant sinners.
The One who commands you to flee immorality is the same risen Christ who gives His people a new life to walk in.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may reveal the consequences of choices you regret.
It may contain chapters you wish you could rewrite.
But it does not have the authority to overrule what Jesus Christ has accomplished through His death and resurrection.
The scandal is real.
The sin is serious.
The wounds may be deep.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is not imaginary.
And for those who turn to Him in faith, the story does not have to end where the shame began.
The hands that were pierced for your redemption are not waiting for you to become worthy of being rescued; they belong to the Savior who came because you could never rescue yourself.
